passage:
Siddharth was five when he wandered into the kitchen after ten minutes of play and announced, "I'm bored. Give me the tablet." Mummy Binita was chopping onions. She did not say no and she did not say yes. She handed him a cardboard tube and a roll of tape. "See what it wants to be." Siddharth sighed loudly. By dinner the tube was a telescope, and he was aiming it at the fridge.
At fifteen, Siddharth stood at the door with his shoes half on. Papa Vaibhav had just said that the family was going to a relative's long afternoon function. "Fiiine," said Siddharth, dragging the word until it was almost a song. His eyes were on the floor. Papa listened to the stretch of the word, then looked at his face. It could have meant "I hate this", or "I'm joking", or "I'm just tired of this kind of afternoon." "That was a long fine," Papa said gently. "Is it fine, or fine-ish?" Siddharth laughed once through his nose. "Fine-ish. It's so slow there." Papa nodded. "Bring headphones for the quiet hour, and we leave after tea," he said.

qa.q: What did Mummy Binita hand Siddharth when he said he was bored?
qa.a: She handed him a cardboard tube and a roll of tape.

qa.q: What links Siddharth's boredom at five with the long "Fiiine" at fifteen?
qa.a: Boredom was the feeling under both. At five he said it in plain words and it turned into imagination, but at fifteen it hid in a dragged-out word, so Papa read the rhythm and the words together and checked gently.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he said "Fiiine" with his eyes on the floor?
qa.a: He felt reluctant and bored, and maybe a little sarcastic, because the slow afternoon did not appeal to him.

qa.q: How could Papa Vaibhav's gentle check help Siddharth?
qa.a: By asking instead of assuming, Papa lets Siddharth say the real feeling and helps them agree on a small plan, like headphones and leaving after tea.

grounding: A child's open boredom at five (4068) later hides in a drawn-out sarcastic-sounding word at fifteen (2532), which a parent reads and checks.
